claims.quote: Form6 can’t be filled by a deleted voter. It’s only for NEW voters.
claims.speaker_note: The first two sentences of the post, verbatim. The FOEJ card renders them 'Form6 can't be filled by a deleted voter. It's only for NEW voters.', which is the same text with straight apostrophes.
claims.relies_on: Rule 13(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 and the title and declaration of Form 6, both as substituted in 2022.
claims.check: Half right. The Rules and the form do frame Form 6 for new electors. Rule 13(1), as substituted by S.O. 2802(E) of 17 June 2022 (in force 1 August 2022, Gazette page 28), reads: 'Every claim for inclusion of name in the roll as new elector shall be in Form 6 and signed by the applicant.' The substituted Form 6 is headed 'Application Form for New Voters' (Gazette page 34; the same title on the PDF the Commission serves at voters.eci.gov.in/formspdf/Form_6_English.pdf, read from Wayback copies of 27 October 2023 and 19 April 2026 whose SHA-1 digests match the archive's records; the repository read the live file on 2 October 2026, forms_primary.json). No document read says a person whose name was deleted may not file it. Section 23(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 gives the right to apply to anyone off the roll: 'Any person whose name is not included in the electoral roll of a constituency may apply to the electoral registration officer for the inclusion of his name in that roll.' Rule 26(1), as amended in 2022, says every application under section 23(1) 'shall be made in duplicate in such one of the Forms 6, 6A, 7 and 8 as may be appropriate' (amendment text from the Commission's letter No. 3/ER/2021/SDR/Vol.II of 23 June 2022, para 3(A)(f), which encloses the Gazette notification). Of those, Form 6A is for overseas electors, Form 7 for objections and deletions, and Form 8 (rule 13(3)) for 'any entry in the roll', which a deleted person no longer has. So Form 6 is the only form for such a person, and the Commission prescribed it. The SIR guidelines with Order No. 23/2025-ERS (Vol.II) of 24 June 2025, para 4(c), say: 'In case any elector is unable to submit their filled in enumeration forms within the specified time, they may file Form 6 alongwith the prescribed Declaration Form (Annexure D) for inclusion during the claims and objections period.' The letter of 1 October 2026 in his own screenshot, para 3, says 'any person not yet enrolled in the electoral roll or whose name has got deleted can apply for enrolment at any point of time', and para 4(ii) tells BLOs to 'facilitate enrolment through Form 6, wherever the person is found to be eligible.' A Commission official quoted by Newslaundry agreed that Form 6 'is meant for new voters' and said: 'If your name has been deleted from the electoral roll, there is no provision for inclusion except through Form 6'. The Rules do not define 'new elector', and a deleted person is not on the roll he applies to join.
claims.site_counts: Across 31 states, 13,39,03,307 names were left off the drafts (data/india/states.json, total.removed). In the 22 states with a final roll, the net rise from draft to final made up at most 14.6% of the names left off at the draft (final.made_up_pct). Every one of those names comes back only through a Form 6.
claims.site_stops: The site holds no count of Form 6 applications from the special drive, and no figure for how many people left off have applied.

claims.quote: All those who have been forced to fill it have committed criminal offence carrying 1 yr prison.
claims.speaker_note: Third sentence of the post, verbatim. FOEJ's card adds 'a' before 'criminal offence'. The post names no section; the one-year figure matches section 31 of the 1950 Act, which Form 6 itself cites.
claims.relies_on: Declaration (iii) of Form 6 and section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
claims.check: The form's wording supports him on one line, and the conclusion goes further than the documents. The declaration of Form 6 as substituted in 2022 (Form 6 as substituted by the Registration of Electors (Amendment) Rules, 2022, Ministry of Law and Justice (Legislative Department) notification S.O. 2802(E) of 17 June 2022, in force 1 August 2022, Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, Section 3(ii), No. 2668, para 10, Gazette pages 34 to 36 (declaration on page 35)) reads: 'I HEREBY DECLARE that to the best of my knowledge and belief- ... (iii) I am applying for inclusion in Electoral Roll for the first time and my name is not included in any Assembly Constituency/ Parliamentary Constituency. ... (v) I am aware that making the above statement or declaration in relation to this application which is false and which I know or believe to be false or do not believe to be true, is punishable under Section 31 of Representation of the People Act, 1950 (43 of 1950) with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine or with both.' Item (iii) cannot be struck off; only item (iv) carries '(Strike off, if not applicable)'. For anyone who was on a roll before, the words 'for the first time' are untrue, and the applicant knows they are. The second half of (iii), that the name is not now on any roll, is true of a deleted elector. Section 31 of the 1950 Act reads: 'If any person makes in connection with— (a) the preparation, revision or correction of an electoral roll, or (b) the inclusion or exclusion of any entry in or from an electoral roll, a statement or declaration in writing which is false and which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.' So one year is the maximum, with a fine as the alternative; it is not a fixed term. The older Form 6 of 2003 carried no such line. Its declaration (iv) read 'my name has not already been included in the electoral roll for this or any other assembly constituency', with an alternative for a name 'included in the electoral roll for ... constituency in ... State in which I was ordinarily resident earlier' (Rules as published by the High Court of Tripura, Form 6 substituted by S.O. 934(E) of 18 August 2003). The 'first time' wording came in 2022. During the SIR, the declarations attached to Form 6 do not ask for it: Annexure D of 24 June 2025 says '(iii) I am applying for inclusion in the Electoral Roll and my name is not included in any other Assembly Constituency/ Parliamentary Constituency', and Annexure IV of 27 October 2025 says '(ii) I am applying for inclusion in the Electoral Roll through Form 6, and my name is not included in any other Assembly Constituency/Parliamentary Constituency' (forms_primary.json). But Annexure D was required 'to support the declaration made therein', so it sits beside the Form 6 declaration and does not replace it. Outside the revision the Commission now uses the Rules form: Press Note ECI/PN/120/2026 of 26 September 2026, decision iii: 'For non -SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used.' So the special drive under the letter of 1 October 2026 runs on the 2022 form with item (iii) as printed. What no document read settles is whether signing it, at an officer's direction and in order to get back on the roll, is an offence. Section 31 needs a statement made knowing it to be false. Whether a court would read that to cover an applicant who signs the Commission's own prescribed form, with every other fact true, is a question for a court. No prosecution under section 31 of anyone re-enrolling through Form 6 was found. 'Have committed criminal offence' is therefore his reading of the law, and no finding supports it. 'Forced' is his word. The letter of 1 October says BLOs 'facilitate enrolment through Form 6' and 'ensure filling up of Form 6'. It contains no compulsion, though for a deleted person it is the only way back.
claims.site_stops: The site does not hold the special drive's own figures, or any case under section 31.

claims.quote: EC officials who forced them are abetters to crime. This press note shows ECI’s abetment!
claims.speaker_note: The last two sentences of the post, verbatim, above the screenshots of the Commission's letter of 1 October 2026.
claims.relies_on: The Commission's letter No. 23/2025/ERS(Vol-II) of 1 October 2026, in his screenshots.
claims.check: The document he attaches is the Commission's letter of 1 October 2026, not a press note. It reads, para 4(ii): 'BLOs shall undertake House-to-House (H2H) visits in respect of such identified electors to ascertain their present status and facilitate enrolment through Form 6, wherever the person is found to be eligible.' Para 4(iii): 'BLOs will also ensure filling up of Form 6 for enrolment of any left out/first time/young electors during their house to house visits.' Para 4(v): 'ERO is the competent authority to act as deemed fit on these cases as per the provisions under The Representation of The People Act, 1950 and Registration of Electors Rules 1960.' The letter does show the Commission directing its officers to have deleted electors file Form 6. Abetment needs an offence to abet, and the second claim above found that no document settles that one was committed. The abetment provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita were not read for this panel. Section 32 of the 1950 Act, on breach of official duty by registration staff, can be taken up only on a complaint 'made by order of, or under authority from, the Election Commission or the Chief Electoral Officer' (s.32(3)). Calling the letter 'abetment' is his charge. The documents show only that the Commission prescribed the form.

strongest_points: Declaration (iii) of the Form 6 in force since 1 August 2022 says 'I am applying for inclusion in Electoral Roll for the first time', item (v) warns that a false statement is punishable under section 31, and a deleted elector cannot truthfully sign the words 'for the first time'.

Rule 13(1) as substituted in 2022 makes Form 6 the form for a claim 'as new elector', and the form is titled 'Application Form for New Voters'; a Commission official agreed the point is technically correct.
Outside the SIR the Commission said on 26 September 2026 that the Rules forms apply, so the special drive ordered on 1 October runs on that form.
overreach: That a deleted voter 'can't' file Form 6: section 23(1) and rule 26(1) give anyone off the roll the right to apply, Form 6 is the only form that fits, and the Commission's orders of 24 June 2025 and 1 October 2026 direct it.

That everyone who filled it 'committed' an offence carrying a year in prison: section 31 needs a statement known to be false, the year is a maximum with a fine as the alternative, and no court has ruled on a deleted elector signing the prescribed form.
That officials 'forced' anyone and are 'abetters': the letter tells BLOs to facilitate and ensure filing, and abetment needs an offence that no document shows was committed.
He calls the attachment a press note. It is the Commission's letter of 1 October 2026.
not_verified: FOEJ's card on Instagram and Threads was not opened; its wording is taken from the request, and it matches the post apart from the article 'a' and straight apostrophes.
The Commission's Manual on Electoral Rolls, which the official quoted by Newslaundry says provides for re-enrolment through Form 6, was not read.
The abetment provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 were not read.
The online Form 6 on ECINET, as it stood during the special drive, was not opened; only the downloadable form and the Gazette form were read.

eci.gov.in refused the sandbox (406), so Press Note 120 and the letter of 1 October were not re-opened today; the press note's words are from the repository's earlier reading (help_research/remedies.json, panels_research/verified.json), and the letter's from the screenshots in his post, which match the repository's earlier reading of it.
The 1950 Act was read in the High Court of Tripura's copy, which predates the 2021 amendments; sections 22, 23(1) to (3), 24 and 31 were not changed by them.
No search of court records for a prosecution under section 31 was made beyond news searches.

claims.quote: After the protests and the notice issued by the Supreme Court, wisdom has dawned on the ECI and Mr Gyanesh Kumar
claims.speaker_note: First paragraph of the post, verbatim, with no full stop.
claims.relies_on: The order for a special summary revision as reported on 15 October 2026, and the Supreme Court's notice of the same day on the INDIA bloc leaders' petition.
claims.check: The two events are real and fell on the same day. A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi issued notice on 15 October 2026 on the petition of Rahul Gandhi, Mallikarjun Kharge and other INDIA bloc leaders against the Commission, the Chief Election Commissioner and the two Election Commissioners (LiveLaw, in disputes.json), after the court had issued notice on 5 October on a petition to quash 14 decisions said to have been taken by the Chief Election Commissioner alone. ANI reported the Commission's letter ordering the summary revision on 15 October (21:10 IST). No reported text of the order gives a reason for it, and none says it was made because of the protests or the notice. Two things in the documents cut against reading it as a retreat. The order, as reported, applies to the 17 states and union territories where the SIR is over (16) or which had a Special Revision (Assam), so it ends nothing that was running. And the Commission had already said on 26 September 2026, before both notices, that 'SIR has already been completed in 20 States/UTs' and ordered a special drive to enrol those left out (ECI/PN/120/2026, para 2). Why the Commission acted is his reading.
claims.site_stops: The site holds the Commission's documents and the court reports, and nothing that shows why the Commission chose this date.

claims.quote: S.I.R. has been abandoned for the 17 remaining States and UTs, and it will only be the customary SSR (special summary revision)
claims.speaker_note: Second paragraph of the post, verbatim.
claims.relies_on: The Commission's letter of 15 October 2026 on a special summary revision with qualifying date 1 January 2027, as reported.
claims.check: The number 17 is the order's, and the states are the other way round. As ANI reported the letter (the letter itself was not read: eci.gov.in answers 406), the summary revision is ordered in Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Kerala, Lakshadweep, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Puducherry, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and West Bengal. PTI's copy (Siasat) says 'In these 17 states, special intensive revision of voters' list is over. In Assam, a special revision instead of SIR took place because of legal reasons.' Every one of the 16 other than Assam has a final SIR roll in states.json, the latest Punjab's of 12 October 2026. So these are the states where the SIR is finished, not the remaining ones, and the summary revision follows it. For the states where the SIR 'is ongoing or has recently concluded, including Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Odisha, Telangana and Delhi', ANI reports the letter says the schedule 'would be announced separately'. No document or report found says the SIR has been stopped in any of the ten states still in it on 24 October 2026 (Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Delhi, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Haryana, Meghalaya and Nagaland awaiting a final roll, and Tripura with no draft yet), and the Chief Electoral Officers of Meghalaya and Delhi still gave SIR dates after 15 October (Meghalaya's site, read 19 October; Delhi's as ANI reported on 17 October). 'Customary' fits: PTI calls it the 'annual special summary revision'. One thing the reports leave unexplained: Odisha, Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Mizoram, Chandigarh, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu also have final SIR rolls and are not among the 17.
claims.site_counts: The SIR covers 32 states and union territories: 31 have a draft roll and Tripura has none yet (states.json). 22 have a final roll. Assam had a Special Revision and is outside the SIR figures, and Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh have no schedule.
claims.site_stops: The site holds no copy of the order of 15 October 2026 and no schedule for the summary revision in the ten states still in the SIR.

claims.quote: Documents to prove citizenship need not be produced
claims.speaker_note: Third paragraph of the post, verbatim.
claims.relies_on: His reading of the change from the SIR to a summary revision. He names no document.
claims.check: No report of the order read here (ANI, PTI in Siasat, The Wire, Outlook) says anything about documents of citizenship. What the site's documents do show points the same way as his line, for new applicants. In the SIR a declaration went with every Form 6: Annexure D of 24 June 2025 in Bihar, with its documents by birth cohort, then Annexure IV of 27 October 2025, which asks for an entry in the last intensive revision's roll (forms_primary.json). The Commission's press note of 26 September 2026 said that outside the revision 'the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used', so on that note the SIR declaration would not go with a Form 6 in a summary revision. PTI reports there will be 'no house-to-house BLO visits' in it. Two limits. The SIR did not ask every elector for documents either: from Phase II no documents were collected with the enumeration form, and notices went to those who could not be linked to the old roll (process.json, 27 October 2025). And the order may say more than the reports carry.
claims.site_stops: The site has not read the order of 15 October 2026 or any instruction on what a Form 6 applicant must file in the summary revision.

claims.quote: Why were 20 States discriminated against under S.I.R.
claims.speaker_note: Opening of the fourth paragraph, verbatim. The paragraph is one question and continues in the next claim.
claims.relies_on: Apparently the Commission's own count: 'SIR has already been completed in 20 States/UTs including Bihar and West Bengal' (ECI/PN/120/2026 of 26 September 2026, para 2).
claims.check: The 20 matches the Commission's count of 26 September, and states.json agrees with it on that date: Bihar, the 12 states and union territories of Phase II, and the seven of Phase III with a final roll by then (Manipur and Sikkim on 6 September, Mizoram on 7 September, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu on 11 September, Odisha on 21 September, Arunachal Pradesh and Chandigarh on 22 September). Uttarakhand (3 October) and Punjab (12 October) have since finished, which makes 22. But the SIR was not confined to them. The order of 24 June 2025 directed it 'in the entire country', starting with Bihar, and it runs in 32 states and union territories, ten of them still in it. The difference he points to is one of timing: the 20 went through the SIR, and the 17 in the new order are, on the reports, mostly the same states going on to a summary revision. 'Discriminated' is his word.
claims.site_counts: In the 20 states and union territories finished by 26 September 2026, 7,48,54,691 names were left off the drafts, of 62,73,15,144 on the rolls before (states.json; 1,77,81,539 of them recorded as dead).

claims.quote: and 13,30,00,000 names (including the dead) were removed without Due Process?
claims.speaker_note: End of the fourth paragraph, verbatim. 13,30,00,000 is 13.30 crore.
claims.relies_on: A count of the names left off the draft rolls across the SIR states; he gives no source.
claims.check: The count is close and its scope is wider than his 20 states. Across the 31 states and union territories with a draft, 13,39,03,307 names were left off, 14.08 per 100 on the rolls before; his 13.30 crore is about 9 lakh below that. The 20 states he names account for 7.49 crore of it, and the other 5.9 crore are in the 11 states that had not finished by 26 September, nine of which were still awaiting a final roll on 24 October 2026. 'Including the dead' is right: 2,79,69,558, 20.9 per 100 of the names left off, were recorded as dead. 'Removed without Due Process' runs two things together. A name left off the draft has not been deleted: the Supreme Court held for Bihar that 'such non-inclusion is not tantamount to a final deletion, but is only a provisional step' (2026 INSC 564, para 134, and para 142). Deletion is an order of the registration officer under section 22 of the 1950 Act, which needs 'a reasonable opportunity of being heard' for anyone said to have moved or to be ineligible, with appeals under section 24. On Bihar the Court held that 'The deletions effected pursuant to the Impugned SIR exercise cannot be said to be contrary to the procedure prescribed under Rule 21A' and that 'The safeguards of notice and hearing are preserved in substance' (para 186(d)). That judgment is on Bihar's revision. Whether each officer gave a hearing in the later phases is what the petitions now pending ask, and the site's figures cannot answer it.
claims.site_counts: 13,39,03,307 names left off the drafts in 31 states, of 95,08,13,771 on the rolls before (total.removed, total.per_100 14.083). Dead 2,79,69,558, shifted, absent or other 9,56,35,923, enrolled more than once 1,01,48,459. After the draft, 33,65,116 names were deleted in the 20 states that published gross figures (after_draft). In the 22 states with a final roll, the net rise from draft to final made up at most 14.6% of the names left off (final.made_up_pct).
claims.site_stops: The site counts names. It cannot say whether a hearing was given in any case, or how many of those left off were entitled to stay.

claims.quote: After removing crores of names illegally, now the ECI has undertaken another exercise to include the 'left out' voters!
claims.speaker_note: Fifth paragraph of the post, verbatim, with straight quotation marks round 'left out'.
claims.relies_on: The special drive for electors left out, ordered on 26 September and set out in the letter of 1 October 2026, and the summary revision.
claims.check: The drive exists. The press note of 26 September 2026 said 'Any person whose name has got left out during SIR or thereafter ... may apply to the concerned ERO' and 'The CEOs, DEOs, EROs will immediately launch a special drive for enrolment of these electors'. The letter of 1 October 2026 tells booth officers to compare the roll from before the revision with the current one, visit those missing and help those found eligible fill in Form 6 (process.json). The summary revision is a separate step with the same aim in its own words: officers 'will ensure that every eligible person ... is enrolled' (as ANI quoted the letter of 15 October). 'Illegally' is his charge. The one judgment on it, on Bihar's revision, held the deletions within the procedure of the Rules (2026 INSC 564, para 186(d)), and the later phases have not been ruled on.
claims.site_counts: In the 22 states with a final roll, 1,13,76,238 names were added on net between draft and final (final.net_after_draft). That count includes new voters.
claims.site_stops: The site holds no count of Form 6 applications from the special drive.

claims.quote: Mr Gyanesh Kumar should be surcharged for the double expenditure
claims.speaker_note: Last paragraph of the post, verbatim.
claims.relies_on: His view that the drive and the summary revision repeat work the SIR should have done.
claims.check: A demand, with no figure to check. The site holds no cost of the SIR, the special drive or the summary revision. The summary revision, on PTI's account, is the annual one, so it is not an expense created by the SIR, and PTI reports it will have no house-to-house visits. Whether any power exists to surcharge a Chief Election Commissioner was not looked into.
claims.site_stops: The site holds no spending figures.

strongest_points: His 20 is the Commission's own count of states where the SIR was complete on 26 September 2026, and the site's records give the same 20 on that date.
His 13.30 crore is within one per cent of the 13,39,03,307 names left off the drafts in 31 states, and about one in five of them were recorded as dead, as he says.

The Commission did order a drive to bring back those left out (26 September and 1 October 2026) and has now ordered a summary revision with the same aim, which shows how many eligible people it expects to be missing.
Outside the revision the Commission said the Rules forms apply, so the SIR's extra declaration should not go with a Form 6 in the summary revision.
overreach: The 17 states in the order are where the SIR is over, not where it remains. The reports say the schedule for the states still in the SIR will be announced separately, and nothing found says it has been abandoned anywhere.

That the Commission acted because of the protests and the Supreme Court's notice: the order gives no reason as reported, and the drive for those left out was ordered on 26 September, before both notices.
He sets 13.30 crore against 20 states. The 20 account for 7.49 crore, and the rest are in 11 states still in the revision.

Names left off the draft are not deletions, and the Supreme Court held Bihar's deletions consistent with the procedure of the Rules. 'Without Due Process' and 'illegally' are his charges, not findings.
No report of the order says citizenship documents need not be produced; that is his inference, though the press note of 26 September points the same way.
not_verified: The Commission's letter or release of 15 October 2026 on the summary revision was not read (eci.gov.in answers 406, PIB reset the connection); its contents are taken from ANI, PTI in Siasat, The Wire and Outlook as gathered in the process update draft of 19 October 2026. The News Mill dates it 14 October.

The post's full text came from api.fxtwitter.com, a third-party mirror of X's data. X's own syndication endpoint carries only the first 279 characters, which match. The News Mill and Organiser quote the rest in the same words.
ANI's report of the post (403) and OpIndia's fact check (challenge page) were not read.

Press Note ECI/PN/120/2026 and the letter of 1 October 2026 were not re-opened today; their words are from the repository's earlier reading (process_research/eci_press_notes_2026-09.md, process.json).
The Form 6 prescribed by the 1960 Rules was not re-read for what documents it asks for.
His offices other than member of the Rajya Sabha and former Finance Minister were not re-read from a primary list.
No power to surcharge a Chief Election Commissioner, and no figure for the cost of any revision, was looked for.

claims.quote: In India, registration is voluntary; you fill in Form 6 if you want to vote. The ECI’s own pre-SIR data showed that in the 2024 Lok Sabha election, one in four Indians aged 18 to 29, 73 million young people, were not registered. Add a small allowance for older adults who have never registered, or who dropped off after moving, and about 8.5 per cent of adults are legitimately not on the rolls.
claims.speaker_note: The second step of his argument in the column, in one passage.
claims.relies_on: The ECI's count of electors aged 18 to 29 on the 2024 roll (ECI Atlas 2024, Table 7.1, and the PIB factsheet of the final roll of 8 February 2024, as his Substack sources list) against his own estimate of the young adult population, plus an allowance of 1 per cent of adults (range 0 to 2) for older adults, which is his judgement.
claims.check: Not recomputable from the site, which holds no roll or population by age. What the site holds sets bounds on it. On the UN's estimate the national roll of 2024 held 97,97,51,847 names against 1,01,76,59,624 adults, 96.3 per 100 (lok_sabha_electors.json), a total gap of 3.79 crore or 3.7 per 100. If 8.5 per 100 adults were not registered, about 4.86 crore names (4.8 per 100 adults) on the 2024 roll would have had to be the dead, duplicates or people registered in two places. Before the revision the nine states' rolls held 58,60,69,594 names against 60,12,56,000 projected adults, 97.5 per 100 (states.json), and across 19 states 98.3 per 100. Tamil Nadu (106.5) and Kerala (100.4) held more names than projected adults, which supports his point that some rolls carried names that should not be there. On voluntariness, section 23(1) of the 1950 Act does say a person not on the roll "may apply" (Form 6), but in an intensive revision the roll "shall be prepared afresh" under rule 25(2) of the 1960 Rules, and the SIR order of 24 June 2025 sent an enumeration form to every elector on the roll (terms.json rpa-s23, rer-r25-2; process.json 2025-06-24). His benchmark treats the young not on the roll in 2024 as a choice, which the data cannot show either way.
claims.site_counts: Roll of 2024 at 96.3 per 100 adults (UN). Nine states before the revision 97.5 per 100 projected adults (58,60,69,594 of 60,12,56,000). Tamil Nadu 106.5, Kerala 100.4.
claims.site_stops: The site holds no count by age and cannot say how many adults chose not to register.

claims.quote: A clean roll for these states, built from each state’s adults less each state’s own non-registration, should hold about 535 million names; the final rolls hold 528 million. Allowing for the legitimate removal of non-citizens, the best estimate is that about 7 million eligible voters (range 1 to 13 million) have been excluded from the rolls without adequate explanation.
claims.speaker_note: The third step of the column. "These states" are Bihar and the eight large states of phase II with final rolls (Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, Kerala), the same nine as Drèze and Yadav's table.
claims.relies_on: Each state's projected adults (Technical Group, July 2020) less that state's own unregistered 18 to 29 year olds in 2024 and 1 per cent of adults, against the final SIR rolls, netting the states above the clean roll against those below, less about 0.5 million for non-citizens.
claims.check: His 528 million (527.8 in the Substack) is the site's nine final rolls, 52,45,53,415, with West Bengal counted at 67.7 million where the Chief Electoral Officer's final roll of 28 February 2026 is 6,44,52,609: 524.55 - 64.45 + 67.7 = 527.80. His 67.7 million matches the final roll plus the 32,68,119 found eligible at adjudication (6,77,20,728), close to the 6,82,51,008 on the roll the 2026 election was held on. His 535.1 million clean roll is 89.0 per cent of the site's 60,12,56,000 projected adults, so it implies 11.0 per cent non-registration across these nine, above his national 8.5, because Uttar Pradesh and Bihar registered only 60 per cent of their young (his figure, not held by the site). With a flat 8.5 per cent for every state, the same final rolls fall short of a clean roll by about 2.56 crore net (2.18 crore with West Bengal on the election roll), and by about 2.88 crore counting only the states that fall short. So the 7 million depends on two choices, state-specific young registration and netting Bihar's, Tamil Nadu's and Kerala's surplus names against shortfalls elsewhere. He explains the netting by migrant workers registered at home, which the site cannot test.
claims.site_counts: Nine states, final rolls 52,45,53,415 against 60,12,56,000 projected adults, 87.2 per 100, a gap of 7,67,02,585 (12.8 per cent).
claims.site_stops: The site holds no registration by age and no count of non-citizens, so it cannot rebuild his clean roll state by state.

claims.quote: The 130 million in the headlines counts every draft removal, in all three phases, before appeals. It is nearly twenty times the number of eligible voters removed.
claims.speaker_note: From the opening summary of the Substack. "Eligible voters removed" is his 7 million (range 1 to 13).
claims.relies_on: The ECI's draft-stage total of 133.7 million names (as Deccan Herald reported it on 30 September 2026) against his 7 million.
claims.check: The site counts 13,39,03,307 names left off the drafts in 31 states (states.json total.removed), against his 133.7 million. 133.7 / 7 = 19.1, so "nearly twenty times" follows from his own two numbers. The two do not cover the same ground. His 7 million is for nine states with final rolls and nets surpluses against shortfalls. The 13.39 crore covers 31 states, nine of them without a final roll on 24 October 2026, and is a draft-stage count before claims. Of the 13.39 crore, 2,79,69,558 were entered as dead and 1,01,48,459 as enrolled more than once.
claims.site_counts: 13,39,03,307 left off the drafts in 31 states. Dead 2,79,69,558. Enrolled more than once 1,01,48,459. Nine states 7,19,68,121.
claims.site_stops: Neither count says how many of those left off were entitled to stay.

claims.quote: But with only 60% of its young registered, a clean UP roll is about 85% of adults, and the final roll is within about 1.4 million of it.
claims.speaker_note: Section 7 of the Substack, on Uttar Pradesh. This is the higher threshold Drèze and Yadav object to.
claims.relies_on: His figure that only 60 per cent of Uttar Pradesh's 18 to 29 year olds were on the roll in 2024 (ECI Atlas 2024, Table 7.1, as he cites it).
claims.check: On the site's figures Uttar Pradesh's final roll of 10 April 2026 is 13,39,84,792 against 16,16,85,000 projected adults, 82.9 per cent (he says 84 per cent, on adults at the roll's qualifying date). A clean roll at 85 per cent of the site's adults is 13,74,32,250, 34.5 lakh above the final roll (he says within about 14 lakh). At his national 8.5 per cent the clean roll is 14,79,41,775 and the final roll is 1.40 crore short of it, which is Drèze and Yadav's 14 million. Before the revision Uttar Pradesh's roll held 15,44,30,092 names, 95.5 per cent of projected adults. For both his 60 per cent and that roll to be right, about 1.70 crore names (15,44,30,092 less a clean roll of 13,74,32,250) among older adults would have had to be the dead, duplicates or people who had moved. The draft-stage entries give 46,23,796 dead and 25,47,207 enrolled more than once, 72 lakh together, with 2,17,03,064 shifted, absent or other. The 40 per cent unregistered that Drèze and Yadav cite is the same figure seen from the other side.
claims.site_counts: Uttar Pradesh final 13,39,84,792, adults 16,16,85,000 (82.9 per cent). Roll before 15,44,30,092 (95.5 per cent). Left off the draft 2,88,74,067, of them 46,23,796 dead and 25,47,207 enrolled more than once.
claims.site_stops: The site holds no registration by age for Uttar Pradesh.

claims.quote: Of the 58 million names removed in these states, 51 million had to go: The dead, the duplicates, those who had moved away for good. Seven of every eight removals were justified.
claims.speaker_note: "Removed" here is the net fall from the rolls before the revision (586 million) to the final rolls (528 million on his West Bengal figure).
claims.relies_on: His clean roll (535.1 million) against the rolls before the revision (586 million).
claims.check: The 586 million is the site's 58,60,69,594 for the nine rolls before the revision. 586.07 - 527.80 = 58.27 million net fall on his West Bengal figure (61.5 million on the CEO's final roll). His 51 million is 586.07 - 535.1 = 50.97, the gap between the old rolls and his clean roll, so it follows from the benchmark and is not a count of reasons. The officers' entries at the draft stage in the nine states give 7,19,68,121 names left off, 1,67,88,487 entered as dead and 51,02,375 as enrolled more than once (2.19 crore together, 30.4 per cent), and 5,00,71,360 as shifted, absent or other. For 51 million to be names that had to go, about 2.9 crore of the shifted, absent or other entries would have to be people who moved away for good or were not real, which the entries cannot show. An officer's reason was written down and no one checked it.
claims.site_counts: Nine states, rolls before 58,60,69,594, left off the drafts 7,19,68,121, dead 1,67,88,487, enrolled more than once 51,02,375, shifted, absent or other 5,00,71,360.
claims.site_stops: The lists record the officer's reason, and no one has checked it against the person.

claims.quote: In 2004, after the last nationwide intensive revision, the roll held 4.4 per cent more names than there were adults, 28 million phantom voters. It was 3.1 per cent too high in 2014.
claims.relies_on: The Lok Sabha rolls of 2004 and 2014 against his census-based adult estimates.
claims.check: The site's own series (ECI Atlas 2024 electors against the UN World Population Prospects 2024, 18 and over, 1 July of the election year) gives the opposite sign. 2004, 67,14,87,930 electors against 67,86,93,381 adults, 98.9 per 100. 2014, 83,40,82,814 against 84,93,20,842, 98.2 per 100. On the UN figures the roll last exceeded the adult population in 1999 (103.4). His 4.4 and 3.1 per cent excess come from his own adult estimate, census carried forward and corrected for a 2 per cent overshoot. The roll counts are the same, so the difference is entirely in the adult denominator, which is also the quantity his 7 million rests on. "Phantom voters" is his word.
claims.site_stops: The site uses one population estimate, the UN's, and says the comparison holds only if the estimate is right.

claims.quote: in West Bengal, 6 to 7 per cent of adults (about 5 million eligible citizens) appear to have been removed without adequate explanation
claims.speaker_note: The sentence continues "; the citizenship-style adjudication fell disproportionately on Muslims in Murshidabad and Malda, and on Matua Hindus." That part is left out because it rests on press analyses of religion that the site does not use.
claims.relies_on: A clean West Bengal roll of 73.3 million (92 per cent of 18 to 29 year olds registered in 2024) against a final roll of 67.7 million, less about 0.5 million non-citizens.
claims.check: The final roll he uses, 67.7 million, is close to the CEO's final roll of 28 February 2026 (6,44,52,609) plus the 32,68,119 found eligible at adjudication (6,77,20,728). The 60,06,675 names held under adjudication were not on the final roll, and 27,16,393 were found not eligible (summary.json adj, as reported). The roll the 2026 election was held on was 6,82,51,008. Against the site's 7,70,30,000 projected adults the election roll is 11.4 per cent short and the CEO's final roll 16.3 per cent. His clean roll of 73.3 million less the election roll gives about 50 lakh, which agrees with his 5 million. The appeals point: 22,21,118 appeals by those excluded, 1,26,194 decided, matches his 2.22 million and 0.13 million.
claims.site_counts: West Bengal final roll 6,44,52,609, under adjudication 60,06,675, found eligible 32,68,119, found not eligible 27,16,393, election roll 6,82,51,008, projected adults 7,70,30,000.
claims.site_stops: The site holds no count of non-citizens and does not use religion splits of those deleted.

claims.quote: the process was hasty, demanded paperwork the poor and the migrant do not keep, and added a new declaration to Form 6 without a change in the rules, a move whose legality the Supreme Court has yet to decide.
claims.speaker_note: His summary of his own column of 24 September 2026.
claims.relies_on: His own experience of the revision and the court and Commission record.
claims.check: The declaration added to Form 6 is in the site's documents (forms_primary.json, Annexure IV of 27 October 2025), and the Supreme Court's remark of 5 October that it "had not approved any modified version of the form" is reported in disputes.json. Stands as his concession.

claims.quote: But criticising the administration of an exercise is very different from claiming that it disenfranchised a seventh of the electorate. The evidence says the ECI has been much more right than wrong.
claims.relies_on: His estimate of 7 million against the 13.3 crore cited by critics. "A seventh of the electorate" is 133.7 million over about 950 million.
claims.check: How he frames the question. 13,39,03,307 of 95,08,13,771 on the rolls before is 14.08 per 100, about one in seven, so "a seventh" matches the draft-stage count.

claims.quote: Put that column back, and DY's own numbers give the answer: About 1 crore disenfranchised, not 7.1 crore. The expected roll is 53.8 crore; the final roll is 52.8 crore.
claims.speaker_note: "That column" is his allowance for adults who would normally not be on the roll, 5.2 crore young people unregistered in 2024 plus 1.5 per cent of adults, 6.1 crore on his 59.9 crore adults.
claims.relies_on: His count of the nine states' projected adults, 59.9 crore, which he presents as Drèze and Yadav's (their printed table gives 601.2 million adults and 530.6 million on the final rolls, 70.6 million short), his count of 5.2 crore unregistered 18 to 29 year olds in 2024 (8.7 per cent of adults), and an allowance of 1.5 per cent of adults for older people, against final rolls of 52.8 crore.
claims.check: On his adults, 59.9 - 5.2 - 0.9 = 53.8, and 53.8 - 52.8 = 1.0 crore. His 59.9 crore adults and 7.1 crore gap are not the figures in Drèze and Yadav's printed table, which gives 601.2 million adults, 530.6 million on the final rolls and 70.6 million short. Their adults equal the site's 60,12,56,000 (states.json adults_2026), which with the same 6.1 crore allowance give an expected roll of 54.0 crore. The site's nine final rolls total 52,45,53,415 with West Bengal at the CEO's 6,44,52,609. On the site's figures the shortfall is 1.57 crore, 1.24 crore with West Bengal after adjudication (6,77,20,728), and 1.19 crore with West Bengal on the election roll (6,82,51,008). On his own 59.9 crore and the site's final rolls it is 1.35 crore. His 17 October column put the figure at about 70 lakh with 59.04 crore adults and a 1 per cent allowance for older people. His clean roll then, 53.51 crore, implies about 4.94 crore young adults off the roll (59.04 - 53.51 - 0.59), against 5.2 crore now, and it also subtracted 5 lakh that the 24 October column does not.
claims.site_counts: Nine states: 60,12,56,000 projected adults, 52,45,53,415 on the final rolls, 87.2 per 100.
claims.site_stops: The site holds no registration by age and cannot test the 5.2 crore or tell a choice from an omission.

claims.quote: West Bengal, where the young register well, expected 7.4 crore and got 6.8: About 60 lakh short. And there the appeals failed: Of the 34 lakh Bengalis who appealed, The Economist reports, fewer than 0.05 per cent had their cases heard before election day, and the tribunals have since found 90 per cent of appellants valid all along.
claims.speaker_note: His only state-level shortfall in the column apart from Bihar's surplus.
claims.relies_on: His expected West Bengal roll of 7.4 crore, the roll of 6.8 crore (close to the election roll), and The Economist for the appeals figures.
claims.check: The site's West Bengal roll: CEO final roll of 28 February 2026 6,44,52,609, election roll 6,82,51,008, projected adults 7,70,30,000. 7.4 crore less the election roll is 57.5 lakh, about his 60 lakh. Appeals in the site's data (westbengal/summary.json adj, from the Commission's affidavit of 16 September 2026 as reported): 38,31,429 in all, 22,21,118 by people excluded and 16,10,311 against inclusion. 1,607 people were restored before the poll (press reports of late April), 0.04 per cent of all appeals and 0.07 per cent of those by the excluded. That is a count of people restored, which is narrower than cases heard, his measure. His 34 lakh matches neither count of appeals. The site holds no figure for tribunals finding 90 per cent of appellants valid. As of the affidavit of 16 September 1,26,194 appeals had been decided.
claims.site_counts: West Bengal: final roll 6,44,52,609, election roll 6,82,51,008, adults 7,70,30,000. Appeals 38,31,429, of which 22,21,118 by the excluded, 1,607 restored before the poll.
claims.site_stops: The site holds no outcome of tribunal decisions after the poll and cannot check the 90 per cent.

claims.quote: Before the SIR, these nine states had 58.6 crore names on their rolls. A clean roll, the table shows, would hold 53.8 crore. The difference, nearly 5 crore names, was the dead, the departed and the duplicated, and this on rolls that still missed 5.2 crore young people.
claims.speaker_note: His case that the old rolls held names that should not have been there.
claims.relies_on: The rolls before the revision, against his clean roll of 53.8 crore.
claims.check: The site's nine rolls before the revision hold 58,60,69,594 names, his 58.6 crore. 58.61 - 53.8 = 4.81 crore. At the draft the officers entered 1,67,88,487 as dead and 51,02,375 as enrolled more than once in these nine states, 2.19 crore in all, of 7,19,68,121 left off. The other 2.6 crore of his 4.8 would have to come from those entered as shifted, absent or other.
claims.site_counts: Nine states before the revision 58,60,69,594. Draft entries: dead 1,67,88,487, duplicate 51,02,375, all left off 7,19,68,121.
claims.site_stops: The site cannot say how many of those entered as shifted or absent had in fact moved.

strongest_points: He separates the draft-stage count of names left off from a count of eligible people kept off, which the site also keeps apart.
His nine final rolls are the site's, his 586 million before the revision is the site's 58.61 crore, and his West Bengal appeals figures match the Commission's affidavit as reported.

He is right that some rolls held more names than projected adults before the revision, Tamil Nadu (106.5 per 100) and Kerala (100.4) among them, so part of any fall was names that should not have been there.
He concedes the process was hasty and that the Form 6 declaration was added without a change in the Rules, and asks the Commission to publish deletions by reason, state and booth.

In his column of 24 October he puts the eligible voters wrongly left off the nine rolls at about 1 crore and lists what the Commission has not published, a national roll after the revision and removals by reason, state and booth.
overreach: His 7 million rests on two choices, a state-specific allowance for young adults not registered and netting surplus states against short ones. With his own national 8.5 per cent applied to each state the nine final rolls are about 2.6 crore short.

His 51 million that "had to go" is the gap between the old rolls and his clean roll. The officers recorded 2.19 crore as dead or duplicate, and the rest would have to come from the shifted, absent or other entries, which no one checked.
He treats the young adults off the 2024 roll as a choice. In an intensive revision the Rules have the roll prepared afresh by the officers.
His 2004 and 2014 excess rolls come from his own adult estimate. On the UN's estimate both rolls held fewer names than adults.
West Bengal is set at 67.7 million, which counts the 32.7 lakh found eligible after the CEO's final roll.

His figure moved from about 70 lakh on 17 October to about 1 crore on 24 October because he changed his count of adults (59.04 to 59.9 crore, which he now attributes to Drèze and Yadav, whose table prints 60.12 crore), his allowance for older people (1 to 1.5 per cent) and his count of young adults off the roll (an implied 4.94 crore to 5.2 crore). On the site's count of adults the same method gives about 1.2 to 1.6 crore.
not_verified: His adult total of 1,008 million for mid-2026 and the claim that the UN, the SRS and the Technical Group all land within 1.5 per cent of it. The site holds the UN's 1,017.66 million for mid-2024, already above his mid-2026 figure, and does not hold the UN's 2026 figure.
The 73 million unregistered 18 to 29 year olds in 2024 and the 60 per cent registration in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar (ECI Atlas 2024, Table 7.1), which the site does not hold.
His per-state clean rolls: the Substack tables did not come through in the saved text.
The religion figures in his West Bengal section and his seat estimates for the 2026 West Bengal election (not quoted).
The Canada, Britain and United States registration comparisons.

pieces.title: Let’s not be in denial — disenfranchisement in real
pieces.how_read: Saved text and HTML read in full on 20 October 2026 (datePublished 2026-10-20T06:22:41+05:30, isAccessibleForFree true). The online headline is kept as published, including "in real". The print edition of the same day, read from a photograph of the page, is headed "Let us not be in denial, disenfranchisement is real" and carries a table the online text does not, "Calculating missing voters in nine major states", with sources "Adult population figures from the report of the Technical Group on Population Projections, July 2020. Final roll figures from ECI press notes and press conferences." Its rows (projected adults 2026, voters on the SIR final list, absolute shortfall in millions, shortfall per cent): Gujarat 53.3, 44, 9.3, 17.4. Uttar Pradesh 161.7, 134, 27.7, 17.1. Chhattisgarh 21.5, 18.7, 2.8, 13.0. Bihar 83, 74.2, 8.8, 10.6. Madhya Pradesh 60.2, 54, 6.2, 10.3. Rajasthan 56.6, 51.5, 5.1, 9.0. West Bengal 77, 70.5, 6.5, 8.4. Tamil Nadu 60.2, 56.7, 3.5, 5.8. Kerala 27.7, 27, 0.7, 2.5. All nine 601.2, 530.6, 70.6, 11.7. The print pull-quote says "well over 10 crore" where the text says "about 14 crore".

claims.quote: We can compare the size of the post-SIR voter lists with official estimates of the adult population that is eligible to vote. Indeed, the ECI itself has been using these population estimates as a benchmark to evaluate its voter lists.
claims.relies_on: The Technical Group on Population Projections (July 2020) for adults in early 2026, against the final SIR rolls.
claims.check: The site uses the same projections (adults_ls2024.csv, the same report) and the same comparison on its All India page. Their adults equal the site's for all nine states. That the ECI uses population estimates as a benchmark (the elector-population ratio of its roll manual) was not read here.
claims.site_counts: Nine states, 60,12,56,000 projected adults.
claims.site_stops: A projection counts residents. It counts migrants where they live, and it counts adults who are not citizens.

claims.quote: For these nine states combined, the voter list falls short of the adult population by more than 7 crore. Almost 12 per cent of the adult population is excluded.
claims.relies_on: The print table: 601.2 million adults, 530.6 million on the final lists, 70.6 million short, 11.7 per cent.
claims.check: Eight of the nine final lists in the table equal the site's final rolls to the rounding printed (Bihar 7,41,92,357, Uttar Pradesh 13,39,84,792, Tamil Nadu 5,67,07,380, Gujarat 4,40,30,725, Madhya Pradesh 5,39,81,065, Rajasthan 5,15,19,929, Chhattisgarh 1,87,30,914, Kerala 2,69,53,644). West Bengal's 70.5 million is the CEO's final roll of 28 February 2026 (6,44,52,609) plus all 60,06,675 names then held under adjudication, 7,04,59,284. Of those, 27,16,393 were later found not eligible, and the roll the 2026 election was held on was 6,82,51,008. So the table understates West Bengal's shortfall by its own method, 8.4 per cent where the election roll gives 11.4 and the final roll 16.3. On the site's figures the nine final rolls hold 52,45,53,415 names against 60,12,56,000 adults, a shortfall of 7.67 crore or 12.8 per cent (7.29 crore and 12.1 per cent with West Bengal on the election roll). Small differences in the table, Chhattisgarh 13.0 per cent against 12.8, Kerala 2.5 per cent against 2.8, come from rounding the final list. Before the revision the same nine rolls held 58,60,69,594 names, 97.5 per cent of projected adults.
claims.site_counts: Nine states, final rolls 52,45,53,415 against 60,12,56,000 projected adults, 12.8 per cent short. Rolls before the revision 97.5 per cent.
claims.site_stops: The gap mixes people wrongly left off with adults never on the roll, and the projection counts residents.

claims.quote: In Uttar Pradesh alone, 2.8 crore are excluded —more than 17 per cent of the adult population.
claims.relies_on: The print table: 161.7 million adults, 134 million on the final list.
claims.check: Site: 16,16,85,000 adults, final roll 13,39,84,792 (10 April 2026), short 2,77,00,208, 17.1 per cent. Agrees. Before the revision Uttar Pradesh's roll held 95.5 per cent of projected adults. Gujarat's shortfall is about as large (17.4 per cent, final 4,40,30,725 of 5,33,01,000), and Gujarat receives migrants, whom the projection counts where they live.
claims.site_counts: Uttar Pradesh final 13,39,84,792, adults 16,16,85,000, 17.1 per cent short.
claims.site_stops: As above.

claims.quote: If the average exclusion rate of 12 per cent for these nine states is representative of the whole country, then the total number of excluded adults or “missing voters” would be around 12 crore.
claims.relies_on: An extrapolation of the nine-state rate to the whole country.
claims.check: 12 per cent of 101.6 crore is 12.2 crore. A conditional extrapolation, stated as such. The nine states hold about 63 per cent of the projected adults in the 19 states the site compares (60,12,56,000 of 95,50,92,000). On the site, the drafts held 84.4 per cent of projected adults across 19 states, and the 22 states with a final roll recovered at most 14.6 per cent of the names left off between draft and final (a ceiling, since it counts new voters).
claims.site_counts: 19 states, drafts 84.4 per cent of projected adults. Final rolls made up at most 14.6 per cent of names left off.
claims.site_stops: The site gives no national figure for adults off the final rolls, because ten states have no final roll yet.

claims.quote: Assuming that these draft lists will undergo the same level of corrections as the first two phases, Rahul Shastri estimates that the final post-SIR voter list for the entire country will be around 87.8 crore. (This estimate does not take into account any corrective action the ECI may undertake from now on to undo the damage). Compare this to India’s current adult population of about 101.6 crore. We are staring at a staggering figure of about 14 crore “missing voters” — adult Indians eligible to vote but excluded from the final electoral rolls.
claims.relies_on: Rahul Shastri's projection of the final rolls from the phase III drafts, and an adult population of 101.6 crore.
claims.check: 101.6 - 87.8 = 13.8 crore, "about 14". Shastri's estimate was not seen. The site holds 95,08,13,771 names on the rolls before the revision in 31 states and 13,39,03,307 left off the drafts, so the drafts held about 81.69 crore, before Assam, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh and before claims. 87.8 crore is in a plausible range on those figures. The adult figure is close to the UN's 1,01,76,59,624 for mid-2024 (lok_sabha_electors.json); the site holds no national Technical Group figure for 2026.
claims.site_counts: 31 states, rolls before 95,08,13,771, left off the drafts 13,39,03,307.
claims.site_stops: A projection of final rolls not yet published.

claims.quote: These disenfranchised voters comprise those eligible voters who featured on the pre-SIR list and were wrongfully removed during the SIR, as well as persons who should have been added to the voter list but were not.
claims.relies_on: Their definition of the gap.
claims.check: An important qualification of their own figures: the gap includes adults never on the roll, so "disenfranchised" here covers both people wrongly left off and people not enrolled. The site keeps the two apart and cannot divide the gap between them. Their "wrongfully removed" is their word.

claims.quote: Voluntary non-registration is not seen as a common phenomenon by the media, political parties or the ECI. Second, voter registration in India has been state initiated. Therefore, non-registration is a failure of the electoral officials that can be rectified, rather than a shortfall to be accepted.
claims.relies_on: Their reading of how registration works in India.
claims.check: Both readings have support in the law. Section 23(1) of the 1950 Act says a person not on the roll "may apply" (Form 6), which is Bhalla's point. Rule 25(2) of the 1960 Rules says that in an intensive revision the roll "shall be prepared afresh", with rules 4 to 23 applied as at first preparation, and the SIR order of 24 June 2025 had enumeration forms carried to every elector on the roll, which is theirs (terms.json rpa-s23, rer-r25-2; process.json 2025-06-24). That voluntary non-registration is not seen as common is their judgement and was not checked.
claims.site_stops: The site holds no measure of how many adults chose not to register.

claims.quote: Indeed, in some earlier years, the enrolment gap among the young was much lower than 7.5 per cent — for example, it was 5.2 per cent of the total adult population in 2014.
claims.relies_on: A count of the young not on the 2014 roll; no source given.
claims.check: Not verifiable from the site, which holds no roll by age. The site's series does show the roll closer to the adult population in 2014 (98.2 per 100) than in 2024 (96.3), which fits a smaller gap then. Bhalla puts 2014 at 3.1 per cent above adults on his own estimate.
claims.site_counts: 2014, 98.2 electors per 100 adults. 2024, 96.3 (UN WPP 2024).
claims.site_stops: The site holds no count by age.

claims.quote: Even if we were to accept Bhalla’s inflated benchmark of 8.5 per cent for voluntary non-registration, there would still be 14 million unfairly excluded voters in Uttar Pradesh alone. This clearly jars with Bhalla’s claim that only 7 million were excluded in the nine states combined.
claims.relies_on: Uttar Pradesh adults (161.7 million) less 8.5 per cent, against the final list (134 million).
claims.check: 16,16,85,000 x 0.915 = 14,79,41,775. Less the final roll 13,39,84,792 gives 1,39,56,983, about 14 million. Arithmetic right. Bhalla's 7 million is not a sum of uniform 8.5 per cent gaps: he uses each state's own registration of the young (60 per cent in Uttar Pradesh), which gives Uttar Pradesh a clean roll at 85 per cent of adults, and he nets Bihar's, Tamil Nadu's and Kerala's surplus names against the shortfalls. Their "breakfast and lunch" point is about the first of these choices. With a flat 8.5 per cent in every state the nine rolls are about 2.56 crore short net, about 2.88 crore counting only the states that fall short.
claims.site_counts: Uttar Pradesh final 13,39,84,792, adults 16,16,85,000. At 91.5 per cent of adults the clean roll is 14,79,41,775.
claims.site_stops: The site holds no count by age and cannot say what share of the young chose not to register.

strongest_points: Their method is the site's own: the final rolls against projected adults from the Technical Group, and eight of their nine state figures match the site's.
Their Uttar Pradesh arithmetic is right on Bhalla's own benchmark: 1.40 crore short at 91.5 per cent of adults.
They state plainly that their gap counts both people wrongly left off and adults never enrolled.
Before the revision the same nine rolls held 97.5 per cent of projected adults, which tells against a normal shortfall as large as 8.5 per cent.
overreach: "Disenfranchised" and "excluded" for the whole gap: the gap includes adults never on the roll, and projections count residents, including migrants where they live and non-citizens.
The national 12 and 14 crore are extrapolations, the second from another analyst's projection of final rolls not yet out.
Tamil Nadu and Kerala held more names than projected adults before the revision, so part of their falls was names that should not have been there.
Their own West Bengal figure counts the 27 lakh later found not eligible as on the list, so it understates West Bengal.
not_verified: The 5.2 per cent young enrolment gap in 2014 (no source given).
Rahul Shastri's estimate of 87.8 crore for the final rolls, and the 101.6 crore adults.
That the ECI uses population estimates as a benchmark for its rolls.
That 40 per cent of 18 to 29 year olds in Uttar Pradesh were not registered in 2024 (it is Bhalla's figure, from the ECI Atlas, which the site does not hold).

pieces.title: Long & short of SIR: What happens when exclusion is prioritised over inclusion
pieces.how_read: Fetched on 22 October 2026 and read in full from the page and its JSON-LD articleBody (datePublished 2026-10-21T23:17:33+05:30, full text served without login). The table is an image, "Ratio of enrolled voters to adult population (%)": all major states 99 before the revision, 85 in the draft lists, final NA. The 12 major states with final SIR lists 97, 86 and 88. Sources "Report of the Technical Group on Population Projections, July 2020, for projected population in 2026; ECI press notes and press conferences for SIR lists. Figures exclude Assam and Himachal Pradesh."

claims.quote: In a recent article in The Indian Express, Yogendra Yadav and I defended the view that the SIR process is leading to mass disenfranchisement - at least 12 cr eligible voters (12% of India's estimated adult population) are likely to be left out of the final SIR lists.
claims.relies_on: The joint column's nine-state shortfall of almost 12 per cent, carried to the whole country.
claims.check: Restates the joint column's extrapolation (see that panel, claims 3 and 4). 12 per cent of 101.6 crore is 12.2 crore. On the site the twelve states with final rolls and projected adults hold 87.5 per cent of projected adults, 8.36 crore short (computed from states.json).
claims.site_counts: Twelve states with final rolls, 87.5 per cent of projected adults.
claims.site_stops: No national figure for adults off the final rolls, since several states have no final roll yet.

claims.quote: For all major states together, pre-SIR lists add up to 99% of the corresponding adult population (see table).
claims.relies_on: His table, rolls before the revision against the Technical Group's projected adults for 2026, Assam and Himachal Pradesh left out.
claims.check: states.json adults: 19 states with projected adults, rolls before 93,92,60,959 against 95,50,92,000 adults, 98.3 per cent. Six held more names than projected adults (over_100: Telangana 115.2, Karnataka 106.8, Tamil Nadu 106.5, Odisha 101.7, Andhra Pradesh 100.7, Kerala 100.4).
claims.site_counts: 19 states, 98.3 per cent.
claims.site_stops: A projection counts residents, so a migrant counts where they live.

claims.quote: 13 cr is the official number of names on 'ASDD lists' - ASDD being 'absentee, shifted, duplicate or deceased' in EC lingo.
claims.relies_on: The Commission's counts of names left off the drafts.
claims.check: states.json total: 13,39,03,307 left off the drafts in 31 states, of which 2,79,69,558 dead, 9,56,35,923 shifted, absent or other, 1,01,48,459 duplicate. Agrees with 13 crore.
claims.site_stops: Reasons are what the officers wrote down, unchecked.

claims.quote: In fact, ground reports from several states (including a careful state-wide survey in Rajasthan) suggest that majority of ASDD deletions are legitimate.
claims.relies_on: Ground reports and a Rajasthan survey the column does not name.
claims.check: The survey is not named and was not seen. Rajasthan's press note (rajasthan summary press.reasons_total): dead 4,61,159, shifted 12,91,846, absent 2,46,249, duplicate 1,53,617.
claims.site_counts: Rajasthan reasons as above.
claims.site_stops: Whether a reason was right needs a check at the door.

claims.quote: In India as a whole, the shortfall is as large as 15% (see table). The gap shrinks when final lists are prepared, but not much.
claims.relies_on: His table: all major states 85 per cent in the draft. Twelve states with final lists 86 in the draft and 88 in the final lists.
claims.check: states.json adults: draft_total 80,65,69,819 of 95,50,92,000, 84.4 per cent, so 15.6 per cent short. Twelve states with final rolls: draft 85.7, final 87.5, or 88.4 with West Bengal's 60,06,675 under adjudication on the roll. The table covers the major states, which the text calls India as a whole.
claims.site_counts: 19 states 84.4 per cent in the draft. Twelve states 85.7 then 87.5.
claims.site_stops: Major states only.

claims.quote: Pre-SIR lists were, in fact, far from inclusive. A significant fraction of the adult population was left out - up to 10% perhaps, judging from patchy evidence.
claims.relies_on: Evidence he calls patchy and does not set out.
claims.check: Not checkable from rolls. Six states held more names than projected adults before the revision, which fits his account of surplus names.
claims.site_counts: Six states over 100 per cent before the revision.
claims.site_stops: The rolls cannot show adults who were never on them.

claims.quote: When a migrant worker is marked as 'Shifted', the largest category in ASDD lists, in their village of origin, there is no guarantee that they have been, or will be, enrolled at the destination point.
claims.relies_on: The reasons officers gave, and the absence of any link between a shifted entry and a new enrolment.
claims.check: Shifted alone is the largest reason in Uttar Pradesh (1,29,77,472, 44.9 per cent), Gujarat (54.6 per cent), Rajasthan (12,91,846) and Bihar (26,55,900 against 22,32,586 dead). In West Bengal dead (24,16,852) exceeds shifted (19,88,076). Most states publish shifted, absent and other together.
claims.site_counts: As above.
claims.site_stops: The rolls do not show whether a person entered as shifted enrolled where they moved.

claims.quote: When the SIR exercise began in June 2025, the most important task was not to weed out surplus names but to include those left out in pre-SIR lists.
claims.relies_on: His judgement of what the revision should have done first.
claims.check: Bihar's order is dated 24 June 2025 (process.json). A judgement, stated as one.

not_verified: The Rajasthan survey, which the column does not name.
The evidence for up to 10 per cent missing before the revision.
